claim: Oil-based Vitamin D3 preparations (liquid drops and softgels) produced 10-25% higher serum 25(OH)D increases compared to dry-powder forms at equivalent doses, per a 2020 systematic review of 11 RCTs.
stance_target: softgels and liquid drops are superior D3 delivery forms vs tablets
scope_conditions: Wagner et al. 2020 systematic review, Nutrients journal, 11 randomized controlled trials
quoted_support: A 2020 systematic review in the journal Nutrients (Wagner et al.) examined 11 randomized controlled trials comparing vitamin D supplement formats and concluded that oil-based delivery vehicles produced superior bioavailability outcomes. The review found mean serum 25(OH)D increases were 10 to 25% higher with oil-based preparations compared to dry-powder forms at equivalent doses.

claim: Liquid Vitamin D3 achieved peak serum levels approximately 2 hours faster than equivalent-dose tablets and showed roughly 12-15% higher overall bioavailability, per a 2019 RCT by Holick et al.
stance_target: liquid/oil-dissolved D3 absorbs faster and more completely than tablet form
scope_conditions: RCT by Holick et al., Journal of Bone and Mineral Research, 2019; liquid D3 vs tablets
quoted_support: A 2019 randomized controlled trial published in the Journal of Bone and Mineral Research by Holick and colleagues found that liquid vitamin D3 preparations achieved peak serum levels approximately 2 hours faster than equivalent-dose tablet forms and produced roughly 12 to 15% higher overall bioavailability. The oil carrier is the key variable.
entities: Journal of Bone and Mineral Research

claim: Oil-based Vitamin D3 preparations raised serum 25(OH)D approximately 20-30% more than equivalent tablet doses over 12 weeks, per Romagnoli et al. 2012 in Osteoporosis International.
stance_target: oil-based forms substantially outperform tablets for D3 absorption
scope_conditions: Romagnoli et al. 2012, Osteoporosis International, 12-week study period
quoted_support: A 2012 study by Romagnoli et al. in Osteoporosis International demonstrated that oil-based vitamin D3 preparations (liquids and softgels) raised serum 25(OH)D concentrations significantly more than equivalent doses in tablet form over a 12-week period. The magnitude of difference was approximately 20 to 30% higher bioavailability for oil-based forms.

claim: Taking Vitamin D with the largest meal of the day increased serum 25(OH)D levels by approximately 50% compared to taking it on an empty stomach or with a low-fat meal.
stance_target: meal fat content significantly impacts D3 absorption from all supplement forms
scope_conditions: Grossmann and Tangpricha 2014 study, European Journal of Clinical Nutrition
quoted_support: A 2014 study published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition by Grossmann and Tangpricha found that taking vitamin D with the largest meal of the day (which typically contains the most fat) increased serum 25(OH)D levels by approximately 50% compared to taking it on an empty stomach or with a low-fat meal.

claim: Softgels dissolve their gelatin shell in 15-20 minutes in the stomach, releasing oil-dissolved D3 with bioavailability comparable to liquid drops but slightly slower onset.
stance_target: softgels are a highly bioavailable, convenient format for D3
scope_conditions: Supplement industry educational content, manufacturer perspective (Mt. Angel Vitamins)
quoted_support: The gelatin shell dissolves quickly in the stomach, releasing the oily D3 solution within 15 to 20 minutes. Bioavailability is comparable to liquid drops in most studies, though the absorption onset is slightly slower because the shell needs to dissolve first.

claim: Gummy vitamins are the weakest D3 form: 2-4g added sugar per serving, lower D3 content per unit, more prone to degradation before expiration, and dental cavity risk.
stance_target: gummies are a high-quality D3 supplement form
scope_conditions: 2017 analysis in Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism on gummy vitamin stability
quoted_support: A 2017 analysis published in the Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism found that gummy vitamins were more likely to degrade before their expiration dates compared to tablets, capsules, and liquids. The sugar-based matrix is more susceptible to heat and humidity.

claim: Vitamin D3 is absorbed in the small intestine via micellar transport alongside dietary fats; forms already dissolved in oil integrate into micelles more readily than dry powder forms.
stance_target: oil-dissolved D3 has mechanistic absorption advantage over dry tablet forms
quoted_support: Vitamin D3 is absorbed in the small intestine alongside dietary fats via the same micellar transport mechanism. When D3 is already dissolved in oil (as in liquid drops and softgels), it integrates into these micelles more readily. When D3 arrives as a dry powder (as in tablets and standard capsules), it first requires emulsification by bile salts and pancreatic lipase activity, and this step is not always 100% efficient.
